messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus was twenty-nine years old, a jeweler by trade, and he had come to understand that the steady, careful work of setting stones and repairing delicate chains was the only thing that still felt safe. He had not always been a jeweler. Three years earlier, he had been a relief worker in a conflict zone, part of a small team that delivered medical supplies and food to villages caught between shifting front lines. The work had been dangerous but necessary, and for the first few months, he had believed that the danger was something he could manage, something with rules. He had been wrong. What happened on the final day was not a single explosion or a firefight. It was a crowd of displaced families, desperate and terrified, pressing against the gate of the compound where his team was sheltering. A child was crying, a high, piercing sound that cut through the shouting. Marcus had tried to help, to open the gate just enough to pass out a crate of supplies, but the crowd surged. He was pulled from the vehicle, knocked to the ground, and for a long, suffocating moment, he was pinned beneath bodies, unable to breathe, his heart hammering so hard he thought it would burst. A hand clamped over his mouth, someone’s knee drove into his ribs, and he was certain he was going to die. He did not die. Someone dragged him back inside. The child kept crying. He never forgot that sound.

In the months that followed, Marcus returned home and tried to resume his life. He took the job at the jewelry shop because it was quiet, because it required fine motor control and deep concentration, and because no one there knew what he had seen. But the quiet did not last. He began to notice that his own body had become a source of alarm. When his heart raced, even from something as simple as climbing stairs or drinking coffee, he felt a surge of panic so intense that he had to sit down, certain that the pounding in his chest was a warning of something catastrophic. He could not be touched unexpectedly. A colleague clapping him on the shoulder, a customer reaching past him to point at a display case, even a friend’s hand on his arm in greeting—each time, he flinched as if struck, his muscles locking, his breath catching. And children crying. That was the worst. A toddler fussing in a stroller outside the shop window could send him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for hours, his jaw tight, his eyes scanning the street for threats that no one else seemed to see.

He developed a set of habits that he told himself were just common sense. He sat with his back to the wall in every restaurant, every waiting room, every bench in the park. He could not eat lunch in the shop’s break room because the door was behind him. He constantly scanned his environment for potential weapons—a pair of scissors on a counter, a heavy glass paperweight, a sharpened pencil—and noted their locations as if cataloging ammunition. When others told him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe them. The words felt hollow, like a script someone had handed him to read, while his own mind insisted that safety was a luxury he no longer had access to. He tried to manage the fear with thoughts he had learned in a self-help book: he reminded himself that it could have been worse, that he had survived, that others had not. He forced himself to think only positive thoughts, repeating affirmations until his temples ached. But the fear did not leave. It only waited.

The memories came without warning. A particular smell in the air, the angle of late afternoon sunlight, the sound of a distant siren—something in his surroundings could instantly bring back the full experience, and for a few seconds, he was back on the ground, the weight pressing down, the child crying. Sometimes the emotion came without any image at all. He would be sitting at his workbench, a loupe in his eye, and suddenly he would be flooded with terror, his hands shaking, his throat tight, and he could not connect the feeling to anything in the present. The memories themselves felt more real than ordinary memories. When he thought about his last vacation, the images were flat and distant, like photographs in an old album. But the memory of that day was vivid, immediate, and alive. It did not feel like the past. It felt like the present, waiting to happen again.

His social life had shrunk to almost nothing. He stopped answering calls from old friends because he could not explain why he had to check every exit before sitting down, why he could not tolerate a hand on his shoulder, why the sound of a child playing in the next room made him want to run. He had not been on a date in two years. The jewelry shop had become his entire world, a small, controlled space where he could manage the variables. But even there, the vigilance was exhausting. He came home each night with sore shoulders and a dull headache, his jaw clenched from hours of scanning, of checking, of waiting.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in the shop when his heart began to race for no reason at all. He was alone, the store was silent, and there was no threat. But his body did not believe that. He stood with his back to the wall, his hands trembling, and for the first time, he understood that he could not out-think this. He did not know if talking could help. He was afraid that it would only make the memories more real. But he was also afraid of living the rest of his life this way, afraid that the only thing he could trust was the feeling of being unsafe. He wanted to believe that there was another way to be in the world, even if he could not yet imagine what it looked like.
